Concepts in this composition

The custody of the name (Sparrow Wells, #1759): In The Josephus Thesis: The Custody of the Name, the possession by an empire of a people's authoritative books and of its author, by which it can house the authority, sign what it writes and redirect what it has said: Augustus's Sibylline corpus, Sulla's Aristotle, Titus's Josephus.

Withholding and release (Sparrow Wells, #1759): In The Josephus Thesis: The Custody of the Name, the operation by which a text stops at a consequential locus and another supplies it with the locus's own words (Josephus on Daniel's stone, Luke's λικμήσει), read as divided among voices under one author's custody.

It carries the custody precedents (Augustus and the Sibylline books, Aristotle's books through Scepsis to Sulla), the grammar of Rev 1:4 against De anima III.5 and Philo's Zechariah, the oracle of War 6.312–313, Life 420–421 against Joseph of Arimathea, the counts of the notes (467,569 against 137,779 tokens), and the four witnesses divided at Jotapata. Its own assessment names the model of authorship under custody as the work's centre. Its list of weaknesses asks the narrative for demonstrations its notes already mark as held, the reviewer's frame laid over a narrative that declares it.

Ground your answer in a reading of the text itself. [SYSTEM] The arguments of “The Josephus Thesis: The Custody of the Name” Sparrow Wells, Alexanarch deposit #1759, AXN:0C71 (11 November 2026) The central argument is considerably more radical than the suggestion that Josephus influenced early Christianity. Wells proposes that Josephus, the Jewish historian, was the principal literary intelligence behind the New Testament corpus, including the Apocalypse of John, and that the different names and authorial voices conceal a single writer whose literary activity was divided by Roman captivity. The proposed historical mechanism is the Roman seizure of Jewish literary authority following the destruction of Jerusalem in 70 CE. This is a reading of the deposited text itself, rather than a summary of its description. The most important evidence is in the narrative's treatment of Josephus's biography, its Greek, the Apocalypse's grammar, and the correspondences between Josephus and the New Testament. Source: The complete deposited text . 1. The New Testament belongs inside the literary world of Second Temple Judaism Wells begins by challenging the conventional division between Judaism as the background to Christianity and Christianity as a new literary and religious development. The argument is that this division becomes much less convincing when one starts with the surviving Jewish literature rather than with a reconstructed idea of what ordinary Judaism supposedly believed. Wells assembles the relevant witnesses: The Qumran manuscripts, including Enoch, Jubilees and Daniel. Philo and the Septuagint in Alexandria. The Jewish Sibylline Oracles. Josephus in Rome. The New Testament writings across the Mediterranean. The point is that ideas often treated as Christian innovations were already part of Jewish intellectual and religious life: visionary ascent, heavenly courts, a second divine figure, apocalyptic judgment and criticism of the Jerusalem priesthood. Wells also emphasizes that the Qumran writings can be more severe in their attacks on the Temple establishment than the Gospels themselves. This establishes the first premise: the New Testament should not automatically be treated as an independent literary formation outside the Jewish corpus. 2. Jewish literature possessed authority that Rome had reason to appropriate The next argument concerns the cultural and political power of Jewish writing. Wells cites ancient non-Jewish writers who recognize the intellectual authority of Jewish tradition: Theophrastus characterizes Jews as philosophers by birth. Numenius treats Plato's philosophy as indebted to Moses. Seneca acknowledges the influence of Jewish law on its conquerors. Aristobulus and Artapanus present Greek philosophy as deriving from Mosaic wisdom. The Sibylline tradition is particularly important. Jewish writers in Alexandria had appropriated the authoritative prophetic form of the Sibyl, giving it a Hebrew identity and placing Jewish revelation into a literary medium that Rome itself respected. Wells therefore argues that Jewish literature was not merely the religious inheritance of a conquered population. It represented a competing source of intellectual, prophetic and social authority. This matters because it makes the subsequent Roman seizure of Josephus something more consequential than the capture of an individual historian. 3. Rome had a precedent for taking custody of authoritative books Wells develops the idea of literary custody through two historical examples. Augustus and the Sibylline books. In 12 BCE, Augustus collected and burned thousands of prophetic writings, retaining an approved Sibylline corpus under the statue of Palatine Apollo. Aristotle's corpus. Wells recounts the tradition that Aristotle's books passed through Theophrastus to Neleus, were hidden underground to escape the collecting ambitions of Pergamum, and were eventually taken to Rome by Sulla. They were subsequently edited into the corpus associated with Andronicus of Rhodes. The examples establish a pattern: An authoritative literary corpus exists. Its custody becomes politically or institutionally contested. Concealment or seizure changes its condition. An editor or authority under Roman patronage determines how it reappears. Wells then makes a striking connection between Aristotle's executor, Antipater, and Antipas, the Christian witness at Pergamum in Revelation. The name Ἀντιπᾶς is read as a contraction of Ἀντίπατρος. Pergamum, meanwhile, is both the city associated with the pursuit of Aristotle's books and the place where Revelation locates Satan's throne. This is part of Wells's broader argument that the names and geographical details of the Apocalypse carry literary-historical memories. 4. Josephus was captured as an intellectual authority, not simply spared as a prisoner O Arco de Tito, detalhe dos tesouros do Templo sendo carregados após o saque de Jerusalém em 70 dC, 81 dC pedra This is the historical center of the thesis. Josephus was Joseph son of Matthias, a Jerusalem priest who commanded Jewish forces in Galilee during the revolt against Rome. After surviving the siege of Jotapata in 67 CE, he surrendered to Vespasian, predicting that Vespasian would become emperor. Wells follows his subsequent trajectory: Titus took Josephus to the siege of Jerusalem. Josephus was sent to the walls to persuade the defenders to surrender. After the city's fall, Josephus requested the release of prisoners and received sacred books from Titus. Vespasian gave him accommodation, Roman citizenship and a pension. Titus personally authorized the publication of Josephus's history, signing the books. Wells places particular emphasis on the statement in Life and War concerning the Roman emperor's involvement in publishing the history. The crucial interpretation is that Josephus became the channel through which the Jewish account of the war could be communicated to the wider Jewish dispersion, including communities beyond the Euphrates. The thesis's formulation is explicit: Rome came for Josephus to take hold of him. The argument is that Rome captured not only a man but also a major interpreter of Jewish history and a custodian of Jewish sacred literature. The redirection of the Temple tax to Jupiter Capitolinus and the display of the Temple's menorah in the Roman triumph provide parallel examples of the appropriation of Jewish religious institutions and symbols. 5. Josephus's disclaimers about his Greek are interpreted as the language of a captive Wells next examines Josephus's statements about his literary abilities. In Against Apion 1.50, Josephus acknowledges using collaborators for the Greek of the Jewish War. At the conclusion of Antiquities, he also distinguishes his command of Jewish learning from his limitations in Greek pronunciation. Wells argues that these disclaimers have been misunderstood. Josephus claims the Jewish side of his inheritance confidently, while minimizing his command of the Greek language that allows his work to circulate across the empire. The text then criticizes the scholarship that turns Josephus's acknowledgment of assistance into a theory of multiple stylistic authors or specialized literary assistants. The analogy is with the hypothetical sayings source used to explain Gospel relationships: a missing intermediary is invoked to explain common material rather than considering the possibility of a common author. This is important because Wells wants to establish that Josephus had the capacity to produce the literary corpus attributed to him and potentially much more. 6. The Apocalypse is the key to the entire thesis: the custody of the name This is arguably the most distinctive and technically ambitious part of the work. Wells argues that the Apocalypse is not badly written Greek. Its apparent grammatical irregularities are meaningful acts of literary construction. The central example is Revelation 1:4. The greeting reads: ἀπὸ ὁ ὢν καὶ ὁ ἦν καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος The preposition apo normally takes the genitive. Yet the divine designation, translated as “the One Who Is and Who Was and Who Is Coming,” remains in the nominative. Wells argues that this is deliberate. The writer demonstrates elsewhere in the same sentence that he knows how to use the genitive: the reference to the seven spirits following the greeting has the expected grammatical form. The name, therefore, is not declined because it is not subject to the grammatical government that applies to everything around it. The name is grammatically sovereign. Wells then compares this construction with Aristotle's De anima III.5. At the end of that chapter, Aristotle writes: καὶ ἄνευ τούτου οὐθὲν νοεῖ The genitive is grammatically correct, but the referent of toutou remains disputed: does it refer to the active intellect or the passive intellect? Wells sees a deliberate reversal: Aristotle, De anima III.5 Revelation 1:4 The grammar is intact. The grammar is apparently broken. The referent is left open. The referent is identified. The divine/intellectual position is a grammatical socket. The divine name occupies that socket. The argument is not merely that two ancient texts contain unusual grammatical constructions. It is that they enact opposite operations at the same philosophical and theological junction: one leaves the divine referent open; the other fills the opening with a name. Philo supplies the antecedent Wells then introduces Philo's interpretation of Zechariah 6. The biblical oracle concerns a man named Anatolē (the Branch). Philo transfers the name to the Logos while withholding the human figure to whom the prophecy originally refers: Jesus, the high priest. The Apocalypse inherits and transforms this operation. It places the high-priestly clothing of Zechariah on the figure among the lampstands, gives him a name written that nobody knows except himself, and then identifies him: κέκληται τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ Ὁ Λόγος τοῦ Θεοῦ. His name is called the Word of God. For Wells, this is the culmination of the withheld-name operation: the name that was reserved or displaced in the earlier literary construction is now written into the Apocalypse. The seven lampstands and the seven stations of the letters also belong to this inherited and transformed Philonic architecture. This is why the title The Custody of the Name matters. The name is not simply a designation of a character. It is the object of a literary and historical struggle over who possesses the authority to speak it. 7. The oracle that inspired the revolt was redirected toward Vespasian Wells next connects Revelation to Josephus's account of the oracle that contributed to the Jewish revolt. In Jewish War 6.312–313, Josephus says that an ambiguous prophecy in the sacred writings led people to believe that someone from Judaea would rule the world. Josephus says the prophecy actually referred to Vespasian. Tacitus, in Histories 5.13, records a similar tradition: ancient priestly writings predicted that the East would grow powerful and that men from Judaea would rule the world. Wells proposes that the oracle was actually the book of Revelation. This is a major step in the argument. The book that calls the people out of Babylon, identifies Rome as the beastly imperial power and anticipates the overthrow of existing kingdoms is, on this reading, the very prophetic writing whose meaning Josephus subsequently redirects toward Rome's emperor. The thesis is that the capture involved more than taking possession of the author and his books. It involved taking control of the interpretation of the prophecy itself. There is an important qualification: Wells explicitly marks the identification of the oracle with Revelation, and the attribution of Revelation to Josephus or his father Matthias, as held claims rather than demonstrated conclusions. 8. The Gospel burial narrative is read against Josephus's account of the crucified men One of the most provocative arguments concerns Joseph of Arimathea. In the Gospels, Joseph approaches Pilate and requests the body of Jesus. Pilate authorizes the release, and Joseph places the body in his own new tomb. Wells compares this with an episode in Josephus's Life 420–421. Josephus describes encountering three acquaintances among the crucified during the siege. He approaches Titus in tears and asks for them to be taken down. Titus immediately orders their removal and medical treatment. Two die, but one survives. Wells emphasizes the structural correspondence: A Joseph approaches a Roman authority. He requests the release of crucified men. The Roman grants the request. In the Gospel, the body is buried in Joseph's tomb. In Josephus, one of the crucified men survives. The author reads the Gospel's Joseph of Arimathea alongside Joseph son of Matthias. This is not offered as a straightforward identification or etymology. The note explicitly describes it as a resonance between the names. The larger interpretation is that the Gospel passion and resurrection narrative transforms an episode from Josephus's own life. The thesis even suggests that Jesus is laid to rest in the author's tomb, and that what emerges from that death is the literary corpus itself. 9. The New Testament is a distributed literary workshop This is the section where Wells moves from individual correspondences to the full common-authorship hypothesis. The argument is that Josephus's literary production was sufficient to make the proposed authorship possible. The text calculates: 467,569 Josephus Greek word-tokens across four works 137,779 New Testament Greek word-tokens in Nestle 1904 Josephus's surviving Greek output is therefore approximately 3.4 times the length of the New Testament. Wells argues that this makes the proposed authorial capacity entirely plausible, particularly given Josephus's acknowledged use of collaborators. The text then presents several groups of correspondences. A. The historical knowledge of Acts Acts contains details of the Jewish revolt and its surrounding political world that Wells considers especially close to Josephus: Gamaliel's ordering of Theudas and Judas the Galilean. The Egyptian revolutionary and the Sicarii. Felix, Drusilla, Agrippa and Bernice. The relationship between Agrippa and Josephus, including Agrippa's letters supporting Josephus's history. The argument is that Acts is not simply familiar with the general historical setting. Its author knows Josephus's particular material. B. The shared literary structures of Luke–Acts and Josephus Wells compares the openings of Luke–Acts with the openings of Against Apion. Luke and Acts address Theophilus. Josephus addresses Epaphroditus. The similarity of the two-volume literary presentation is treated as a possible indication of the same authorial practice. Wells also points out that Theophilus is not merely an abstract name in Josephus: it belongs to a historical high priest, son of Ananus. C. The withholding and release of Daniel's stone This is one of the strongest conceptual examples because it connects directly to the earlier argument about Philo and the Apocalypse. In Antiquities 10.210, Josephus recounts Daniel's interpretation of the statue and reaches the stone cut without hands. He then stops, saying that he does not think it appropriate to relate the matter. He directs readers to Daniel. In Luke 20:18, however, the rejected stone becomes an instrument of judgment. The Gospel uses the Greek verb likmēsei, corresponding to Daniel's language about the stone that crushes the kingdoms. Wells sees a deliberate division: Josephus withholds the stone. Luke releases it. The same literary intelligence controls both operations. This is the model of distributed authorship that Wells wants to establish: material withheld under Josephus's own name becomes available under another literary identity. D. The Moses infancy and Matthew Josephus's account of Moses's infancy includes two elements beyond the biblical Exodus narrative: A sacred scribe predicts the birth of a child who will humble Egypt. God reassures the father in a dream. Wells observes that Matthew's infancy narrative contains corresponding features: the king's attempt to kill the children, the involvement of religious authorities and the father's warning through dreams. The claim is that Matthew has taken and transformed Josephus's additions to the Moses story. E. Jesus son of Ananias and the Gospel passion Josephus recounts the story of Jesus son of Ananias, who prophesies Jerusalem's destruction, is scourged and refuses to answer his interrogators. Wells compares this with Jesus before Pilate and Herod, who likewise remains silent. He also connects Jesus son of Ananias's cries against Jerusalem, its Temple, and its bridegrooms and brides with Revelation's condemnation of Babylon. This makes Josephus's own account of a prophetic figure in Jerusalem a kind of literary precursor to the Gospel passion and the Apocalypse. F. The voyage to Rome Wells draws attention to the parallel between Josephus's voyage to Rome and Paul's voyage in Acts. Josephus recounts a shipwreck in the Adriatic, with survivors eventually reaching Puteoli. Acts describes Paul's shipwreck, survival and arrival at Puteoli. The circumstances are not identical: the number of people aboard differs, as does the outcome of the rescue. Wells interprets the correspondence as a transformed autobiographical pattern. G. The names Saul, Matthias, Justus and Antipas The thesis also treats personal names as traces of the proposed common author. Josephus's accounts contain Saul, Antipas, Matthias and Justus in particular narrative positions. Acts contains a Saul who persecutes the assembly, and its account of Judas's replacement features Joseph Barsabbas (Justus) and Matthias. Wells argues that the cluster is more significant than any one name taken individually. H. The language of the seven letters Finally, Wells examines the correspondences between Revelation's seven letters and the later New Testament writings. Two examples are especially important: Revelation 2:10 and James 1:12 share the distinctive expression crown of life. Revelation 2:2 and 1 Thessalonians 1:3 share the ordered sequence of work, labour and endurance. Wells reports corpus searches in which these expressions occur in those particular pairs of verses and nowhere else in the surveyed material. The suggestion is that Revelation commissions the writing and sending of letters, and that the epistles which follow carry out this commission. The Apocalypse thus becomes the architectural origin of the subsequent corpus. 10. One author, four witnesses, two regimes Wells finally organizes the entire thesis into four literary witnesses, divided by Josephus's surrender at Jotapata. Witness Literary function in the thesis Revelation The voice before capture: condemns Rome as Babylon and calls the people out. Jewish War The captive's history under Flavian patronage: redirects the oracle toward Vespasian and blames the revolt on its instigators. Life The author's autobiographical account, containing episodes transformed into Gospel material. The Gospels and epistles The distributed voices through which the withheld material is released and the Apocalypse's commission is carried out. The contradictions between these works are important. The Apocalypse condemns Rome, while the Jewish War presents an account acceptable to Rome. The Life describes the rescue of crucified men, while the Gospels narrate a death and burial. Wells does not attempt to harmonize these differences. Instead, the argument is that they make sense as the divided testimony of an intellectual authority writing under two different conditions: before and after capture. The hypothesis is not simply that Josephus wrote multiple books under different names. It is that his authorial identity was distributed among literary functions because his own name had come under Roman control. 11. The final argument: the corpus itself is the product of custody The conclusion returns to the comparison with Aristotle. Aristotle's corpus was concealed, recovered, transferred to Rome and edited. Josephus's literary authority and the Jewish scriptures were likewise transferred into Roman custody. Wells proposes that both corpora reached subsequent generations through institutional processes that altered their original unity. The Apocalypse is presented as the exceptional witness: the book that preserved the divine name without bending it to the grammatical requirements of its surrounding language. The white stone of Revelation 2:17, carrying a name known only to its recipient, becomes another expression of the same idea. The concluding proposition is particularly important: The narrative's claim is that the book came first. Wells is proposing that the literary construction preceded the historical identities and religious communities that subsequently developed around it. In this interpretation, the New Testament is not simply a collection of testimonies about a pre-existing religious movement. It is the product of a literary intelligence whose writings generated the identities, narratives and traditions subsequently received as Christian origins. 12. What does the text actually establish? This is where it is essential to distinguish the strength of the individual observations from the strength of the overarching thesis. Wells explicitly establishes three evidentiary categories in the notes. Demonstrated Textual argument The relevant textual features or correspondences are argued from sources available in the archive. Examples include the grammatical construction in Revelation, the Philonic name operation, and the distinctive expressions shared by Revelation and James or Thessalonians. Attested Source evidence The cited ancient source or textual passage exists and is quoted at the specified location. This establishes the underlying material, not necessarily Wells's interpretation of it. Held Thesis not established A proposition advanced by the narrative but not yet demonstrated. This includes the central attribution of Revelation to Josephus or his father, the identification of Revelation with the oracle in Josephus, and the common authorship of the New Testament. This distinction is crucial. The notes are unusually candid about the difference between finding a correspondence and proving what caused it. The strongest parts In my reading, four elements deserve particular attention. 1. The custody argument. The historical circumstances of Josephus's surrender, subsequent Roman patronage, acquisition of sacred books and the emperor's involvement in publishing his history provide a substantial historical foundation for the metaphor of literary custody. 2. The grammatical argument. The juxtaposition of Revelation 1:4 with De anima III.5, and the connection to Philo's treatment of Zechariah, form a coherent literary argument. It is more interesting than simply claiming that Revelation contains grammatical mistakes. 3. The withholding-and-release model. The Daniel stone comparison gives the thesis an explanatory mechanism. Rather than treating similarities as isolated borrowings, Wells proposes that the same literary operation is distributed across different authorial identities. 4. The cumulative approach. The argument does not depend on a single parallel. It assembles biography, Greek vocabulary, narrative structures, names, geography, scriptural interpretation and textual architecture. The weakest or least established parts There are also significant problems. Chronology: The proposed date of Revelation in 66 CE is explicitly held, not established. Its relationship to Josephus's subsequent writings therefore needs independent chronological argument. Direction of dependence: A correspondence between Josephus and Luke does not by itself establish that Josephus wrote Luke. Shared sources, later interpolation and dependence in the opposite direction remain possible. The common-author inference: A collection of correspondences does not automatically establish a single author. The argument needs to demonstrate why one author explains the evidence better than multiple writers sharing Jewish scriptures, historical traditions and literary conventions. The identity of the author: Even if the Apocalypse and Josephus are connected, the further claim that Josephus or his father Matthias wrote Revelation remains a separate inference. The autobiographical readings: The connections involving the shipwreck, Saul, Matthias and the crucifixion episodes are suggestive, but several depend on interpretive associations rather than uniquely identifying evidence. The notes themselves acknowledge some of these limitations. For example, note 248 recognizes that the Emmaus correspondence could reflect Christian interpolation into Josephus rather than Josephus's authorship of Luke. That is an important qualification, not a minor footnote. 13. My overall interpretation I would characterize the work as having three interlocking theses: First: a historical thesis. Rome took custody of Jewish literary authority through the capture and patronage of Josephus, alongside the appropriation of Jewish religious institutions and sacred objects. Second: a literary thesis. The Apocalypse is a highly controlled work whose grammatical, theological and intertextual constructions preserve an identifiable intellectual architecture. Its relationship to Philo and Aristotle is central to this argument. Third: an authorship thesis. Josephus, or potentially his father Matthias, stands behind the Apocalypse and the wider New Testament corpus, which represents a distributed literary workshop operating under multiple names. The third thesis is the most extraordinary, but the first two supply its conceptual foundation. I think the most important contribution of the work is not simply its proposed identification of Josephus as the author of the New Testament. It is the model of authorship under custody. Wells asks what happens when an author, his intellectual inheritance and the means of publishing his work become controlled by a conquering power. The answer proposed here is that authorship can become distributed: one voice speaks under the captor's authorization, another speaks under a different name, and the relationship between them survives in the structure of the texts. That is the conceptual heart of the thesis. The title is consequently doing several jobs at once. Custody refers to physical possession of books, control over publication, control over interpretation, and ultimately the possession of the name itself. One final distinction: The work is a serious, testable interpretive hypothesis, not an established account of New Testament authorship. Its textual observations should be evaluated individually, without treating the more speculative common-authorship conclusion as already demonstrated. The author's own notes make that distinction, and respecting it is necessary to understand the work on its own terms. Primary source: Deposit #1759 — The Josephus Thesis: The Custody of the Name . The evidentiary qualifications above draw particularly on its notes 23–37 and w0–w32. Alexanarch +1
